Circuit Privacy for FHEW/TFHE-Style Fully Homomorphic Encryption in Practice (https://cic.iacr.org/p/1/4/33/pdf)

L0@P0: IACR Communications in Cryptology
L1@P0: ISSN 3006-5496, Vol. 1, No. 4, 40 pages.
L2@P0: https://doi.org/10.62056/av11c3w9p
L3@P0: Check for updates
L4@P0: Circuit Privacy for FHEW/TFHE-Style Fully
L5@P0: Homomorphic Encryption in Practice
L6@P0: Kamil Kluczniaka
L7@P0: Independent Researcher, Munich, Germany
L8@P0: Abstract. A fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme allows a client to encrypt
L9@P0: and delegate its data to a server that performs computation on the encrypted data
L10@P0: that the client can then decrypt. While FHE gives confidentiality to clients’ data, it
L11@P0: does not protect the server’s input and computation. Nevertheless, FHE schemes are
L12@P0: still helpful in building delegation protocols that reduce communication complexity,
L13@P0: as the ciphertext’s size is independent of the size of the computation performed on
L14@P0: them.
L15@P0: We can further extend FHE by a property called circuit privacy, which guarantees
L16@P0: that the result of computing on ciphertexts reveals no information on the computed
L17@P0: function and the inputs of the server. Thereby, circuit private FHE gives rise to round
L18@P0: optimal and communication efficient secure two-party computation protocols. In this
L19@P0: work, we design a randomized FHEW/TFHE-style bootstrapping algorithm whose
L20@P0: single invocation sanitizes a ciphertext and, consequently, serves as a tool to provide
L21@P0: circuit privacy. We give an extensive analysis, propose parameters, and provide a C++
L22@P0: implementation of our scheme. Our bootstrapping can sanitize a ciphertext to achieve
L23@P0: circuit privacy at an 80-bit statistical security level in between 1.3 and 0.9 seconds,
L24@P0: depending which Gaussian sampling algorithm is used, and whether the parameter
L25@P0: set targets a fast Fourier or a number theoretic transform-based implementation. In
L26@P0: addition, we can perform non-sanitized bootstrapping in around 0.27 or 0.14 seconds.
L27@P0: Crucially, we do not need to increase the parameters to perform computation before
L28@P0: or after sanitization takes place. For comparison’s sake, we revisit the Ducas-Stehlé
L29@P0: washing machine method. In particular, we give a tight analysis, estimate efficiency,
L30@P0: review old, and provide new parameters.
L31@P0: Keywords: Fully Homomorphic Encryption · Circuit Privacy
L32@P0: 1 Introduction
L33@P0: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) is an encryption scheme that allows performing
L34@P0: arbitrary computation on encrypted data. A client encrypts a message m and sends the
L35@P0: ciphertext to a server which, given a function F, returns another ciphertext that decrypts
L36@P0: to F(m). The concept of FHE was first introduced by Rivest, Adleman and Dertouzos
L37@P0: [RAD78], and the first theoretical realization of that concept is due to Gentry [Gen09b].
L38@P0: A critical property for FHE is circuit privacy (also called function privacy). Roughly
L39@P0: speaking, the ciphertext that is the product of the server computing a function F on
L40@P0: encrypted data should not reveal any information about F except that the ciphertext
L41@P0: decrypts to F(m). To prove circuit privacy, we need to show a simulator that, on input
L42@P0: F(m) and a public key, outputs a fresh encryption of F(m), which is indistinguishable
L43@P0: E-mail: kamil.kluczniak@gmail.com (Kamil Kluczniak)
L44@P0: aAuthor was partially supported by the German Ministry for Education and Research through funding
L45@P0: for the project CISPA-Stanford Center for Cybersecurity (Funding number: 16KIS0927).
L46@P0: This work is licensed under a “CC BY 4.0” license.
L47@P0-1: Received: 2024-10-09 Accepted: 2024-12-032 Circuit Privacy of FHEW/TFHE-Style FHE Schemes in Practice
L48@P1: from the servers’ computed ciphertext. In particular, the distribution of an evaluated
L49@P1: ciphertext should be close to or the same as the distribution of a fresh encryption.
L50@P1: We can easily see that circuit private FHE gives us semi-honest two-party computation
L51@P1: with optimal communication. Namely, we only need one round of communication. The first
L52@P1: message can be reused, and the communication complexity is independent of the size of the
L53@P1: computation. Furthermore, we can reuse the ciphertexts output from the evaluation process
L54@P1: and keep computing on them. Since circuit private FHE gives us two-party computation,
L55@P1: all applications for two-party computation protocols apply here as well. Among other these
L56@P1: are private set intersection [HFH99, Mea86, CLR17], oblivious pseudorandom functions
L57@P1: [BIP+18, ADDG24] neural network inference [DGBL+16, CdWM+17, LJLA17, JKLS18,
L58@P1: JVC18, BGGJ20, ABSdV19, CDKS19, RSC+19, BGPG20] or analysis on genomic data
L59@P1: [KSK+18, KSK+20, BGPG20]. Recently, Akavia, Gentry, Halevi, and Vald [AGHV22]
L60@P1: showed that circuit private IND-CPA secure homomorphic encryption satisfies a relaxed
L61@P1: notion of CCA2 security. Note that circuit privacy is not always needed. Without
L62@P1: circuit privacy FHE reduces to secure delegation. For example, in (single-server) private
L63@P1: information retrieval we are only interested in protecting the user’s query, but not in the
L64@P1: confidentiality of a potentially large database of the server. On the other hand, we believe
L65@P1: that for neural network inference, as an example, confidentiality of the neural network
L66@P1: is essential. In contrast to PIR, it is difficult to make an argument for compressing the
L67@P1: communication, as current FHE schemes require sending public keys and ciphertexts that
L68@P1: are an order of magnitude larger than the size of deep neural networks.
L69@P1: Despite over a decade of advances in constructing scalable fully homomorphic encryption
L70@P1: schemes [GH11, BV11, BGV12, GHS12, AP13, GSW13, BV14, AP14, HS15, DM15,
L71@P1: CGGI16a, CH18, CGGI20, HS21], and numerous implementations [PAL21, CGGI16b,
L72@P1: CJL+20, Lat22] there are few constructions and implementation that we are aware of
L73@P1: that natively provide circuit privacy.
L74@P1: Current approaches to Circuit Privacy. In this paper, we are interested in fully
L75@P1: homomorphic encryption as in [Gen09b]. Namely, ciphertexts do not grow with the size
L76@P1: of computation, and evaluation results are reusable. A trivial way to re-randomize a
L77@P1: ciphertext is to create a fresh encryption of zero using the public key and add it to the
L78@P1: ciphertext resulting from the computation. Unfortunately, such an approach is insufficient
L79@P1: to provide circuit privacy in current FHE schemes because all secure FHE schemes we
L80@P1: know are based on noisy encryptions. This noise may depend on the computed circuit
L81@P1: and is the main obstacle to overcome when re-randomizing (or sanitizing) a ciphertext to
L82@P1: provide circuit privacy. Below we summarize current approaches.
L83@P1: Noise Flooding: The technique requires adding a fresh ciphertext of zero and a
L84@P1: exponentially larger noise term to the sanitized ciphertext. Unfortunately, in practice, this
L85@P1: additional noise term is substantially large and requires us to choose very big parameters.
L86@P1: We note that it is required to take the noise exponentially larger than the noise in the
L87@P1: sanitized ciphertext due to the smudging lemma [AJL+12]. Hence, if the noise in this
L88@P1: ciphertext is already large due to some previous computation, then the the magnitude of
L89@P1: the additional noise must be chosen accordingly. Nevertheless, the method has found some
L90@P1: applications in leveled homomorphic computation [CLR17] where we do not bootstrap the
L91@P1: ciphertexts and can tolerate larger parameters.
L92@P1: Ducas-Stehlé Washing Machine: Introduced by Ducas and Stehlé [DS16], requires
L93@P1: to run a sequence of re-randomization steps (flooding cycles), each with a smaller noise
L94@P1: flooding error, followed by invocations of a bootstrapping algorithm. The paper only
L95@P1: roughly estimates the number of times re-randomization and bootstrapping must be
L96@P1-2: invoked. However, as the authors admit, the estimates should be taken with great cautionKamil Kluczniak 3
L97@P2: and defer a concrete analysis to future work. For example, they suggest running the
L98@P2: FHEW [DM15] bootstrapping algorithm between 8 and 16 times. It is not entirely clear
L99@P2: what security level they are able to achieve and whether the parameter set of the FHEW
L100@P2: algorithm proposed at the time satisfies the given correctness constraints. To the best of
L101@P2: our knowledge, no concrete analysis or implementations have been done so far.
L102@P2: Secure Two-Party Computation: A few works [OPP14, GHV10, CO17] proposed
L103@P2: to use garbled circuit-based techniques to provide circuit privacy. For example, Gentry,
L104@P2: Halevi, Vaikuntanathan [GHV10] give a non-compact homomorphic encryption scheme that
L105@P2: can be thought of as a re-randomizable version of garbled circuits, which can be instantiated
L106@P2: from the DDH assumption. [GHV10] shows how to make the scheme compact, by performing the evaluation over a compact FHE scheme and using the circuit-private scheme
L107@P2: to re-encrypt the ciphertext. Ostrovsky, Paskin-Cherniavsky and Paskin-Cherniavsky
L108@P2: [OPP14], and Chongchitmate and Ostrovsky [CO17] use the same technique as [GHV10]
L109@P2: to build a compact FHE by sanitizing the ciphertext using a non-compact 2PC scheme,
L110@P2: but to achieve malicious security, they prove the well-formedness of the ciphertext using
L111@P2: zero-knowledge proofs.
L112@P2: Rerandomizing Computation: Bourse, del Pino, Minelli and Wee [BdPMW16]
L113@P2: exploits properties of the Gentry, Sahai, Waters (GSW) cryptosystem [GSW13] to build
L114@P2: a circuit private homomorphic encryption scheme. Specifically, when multiplying GSW
L115@P2: ciphertexts, they use a randomized version of gadget decomposition instead of a deterministic one. In [BdPMW16] the authors show that when gadget decomposition is implemented
L116@P2: via Gaussian sampling [MP12, GM18] with appropriate parameters, then we can build
L117@P2: an FHE scheme for circuits in NC1(circuit of depth logarithmic in the number of inputs).
L118@P2: The results are asymptotic, without concrete parameter proposals nor implementation.
L119@P2: 1.1 Our Contributions
L120@P2: We design a randomized FHEW/TFHE-style [DM15, CGGI16a] bootstrapping algorithm
L121@P2: that can sanitize a given ciphertext. In contrast to the Ducas-Stehlé washing machine
L122@P2: method [DS16], which we shortly refer to as DS-WM, we need to run our bootstrapping
L123@P2: algorithm only once. Our results solve an open problem posted in [BdPMW16], in
L124@P2: that we use their randomization concept in an FHEW-style bootstrapping scheme. We
L125@P2: note that porting the ideas from [BdPMW16] to the ring setting is non-trivial since
L126@P2: there is no analogue of the Gaussian leftover hash lemma [AGHS13, AR13, BdPMW16]
L127@P2: for the ring setting. Moreover, we can argue that designing a “leaky” analogue of the
L128@P2: regularity lemmas [Mic02, SS11, LPR13] as in [DSGKS21], may result in practically
L129@P2: inefficient bootstrapping. While we use some techniques from [BdPMW16], the overall
L130@P2: method departs from [BdPMW16]. In this work we show how to bypass the need to
L131@P2: port [BdPMW16] into the ring setting using simple techniques in the right places by
L132@P2: exploiting structural properties of FHEW/TFHE [DM15, CGGI16a] instantiated over the
L133@P2: ring RQ = ZQ[X]/(XN + 1) where N is a power of two. Along the way, we generalize the
L134@P2: technical lemmas from [BdPMW16] to support any modulus Q ∈ N, instead of moduli of
L135@P2: the form Q = L
L136@P2: ℓ
L137@P2: for some L, ℓ ∈ N.
L138@P2: We compare our method with DS-WM that is the most competitive. While [DS16]
L139@P2: gives a heuristic instantiation based on FHEW [DM15], they left a serious analysis as
L140@P2: an open problem. We resolve the problem and give a tight error analysis, and provide
L141@P2: scripts that automate noise and security estimations of our randomized bootstrapping and
L142@P2: DS-WM. We show that the parameters proposed in [DS16] cannot be circuit private due
L143@P2: to correctness issues. In general, we show that instantiations over a ring of dimension
L144@P2: 2
L145@P2-3: 10, or smaller, cannot give more than 30-bits of statistical security. Note that many4 Circuit Privacy of FHEW/TFHE-Style FHE Schemes in Practice
L146@P3: efficient bootstrapping schemes [DM15, CGGI16a, CGGI20] are instantiated over rings of
L147@P3: dimension 2
L148@P3: 10
L149@P3: .
L150@P3: Finally, we give an efficient C++ implementation1 of our bootstrapping algorithms.
